title: What Really Happens When You Click Login?

timeline.hear: The API Gateway is the first stop for our login request after it crosses the network. It doesn't check your password. Instead, it checks whether the request can continue and where it should go next. And if something is wrong, the login can stop right here.
timeline.voiceDirection: Calm, conversational, confident. Open with API Gateway immediately; pause naturally between the three ideas. Preserve 1.25 seconds of pre-voice silence.

visual.summary: API Gateway appears as the first named subject. Canonical green login request approaches its first server-side stop; Gateway checks permission to continue and next-hop selection, not password validity.

timeline.hear: The request must find the right service. The app now uses version two of the login address. But the gateway still knows only version one. It answers 404. The password check never starts. Choosing where a request goes is called routing.
timeline.voiceDirection: Leave a beat after “Auth Service” so the correct path can be read. Change to diagnostic tone on the deployment mismatch; let the rejection land.

visual.summary: Teach ROUTING with a concrete service path, not with five glossary rows. Green POST /api/v1/login follows the visible route to auth-service. Create ONE amber illustrative request with POST /api/v2/login; let it reach the route fork and halt at a missing path. Illuminate the gap and 404 result; visibly show auth-service has received NO CALL for that failed sample. Only after the cause and failure are visible reveal ROUTING.

timeline.hear: The address is right, but the app sends GET instead of POST. The gateway answers 405: Method Not Allowed. POST is for sending login details. GET asks to read data. This difference is called the HTTP method.
timeline.voiceDirection: Give separate weight to POST and GET. Brief hold after “method not allowed”. Pronounce method names as words, not symbols.

Animate both outcomes before bringing up HTTP METHOD. Separate this from route mismatch visually by keeping address text absolutely unchanged.

timeline.hear: The app gets no answer, so it tries again and again. Soon, too many requests arrive. The gateway answers 429: Too Many Requests. A few quick requests are fine. That is a burst. A limit per minute is a quota. Together, these rules are called rate limiting.
timeline.voiceDirection: Slower for Burst and Quota, then accelerate slightly on “hundreds of automatic retries” and hold on the fact Auth Service is healthy.

visual.summary: Follow one failed illustrative attempt being retried too aggressively. Animate packet arrivals stacking into a small traffic queue, counter 12/100 rising to 124/100 requests/min and the overflow diverting to a red 429 lane. Show separate short burst allowance (5/10 s) and minute quota. Keep the real green request safely away from the overflow. Auth Service in background remains HEALTHY but never receives rejected samples. Reveal RATE LIMIT last.

timeline.hear: Some requests look unsafe. A rule stops them. But a bad rule can also stop a normal login. The gateway answers 403: Forbidden. This kind of check is done by a Web Application Firewall, or WAF.
timeline.voiceDirection: Explain WAF naturally. Pause after “legitimate login”; a clear contrast between a correct request and a false positive.

visual.summary: A green normal login safely passes policy. A separate amber normal-looking example meets an overly broad rule WAF_LOGIN_1042; outline the matched rule and block the otherwise valid sample with 403. Contrast green allowed route and red denied illustrative route; password validation stays unlit. Name WAF after seeing why a false positive matters.

timeline.hear: The app should send a field called email. After an update, it sends userEmail instead. The gateway cannot find the field it needs, so it answers 400: Bad Request. This check is called schema validation.
timeline.voiceDirection: Give viewers time to compare email and userEmail; emphasize that this is a field-name mismatch, not incorrect credentials.

visual.summary: Use a quiet two-column JSON shape comparison in the one active diagnostic area. EXPECTED {"email":"..."} and RECEIVED {"userEmail":"..."}; spotlight the differing field names while everything else dims. Validator searches for email and finds none; a short trace moves to 400 Bad Request. This validator is explicitly configured at the gateway. Never show actual credentials or pretend that every gateway validates JSON.

timeline.hear: Those failures were only examples. Our green request passes. Now it reaches another decision: which healthy server should receive it?
timeline.voiceDirection: Soft reassuring handoff. Pause 0.45s after "examples." and 0.65s after "passes." End on a curious question leading to Load Balancer; do not introduce the next term early.
